Geologists have long considered such regions too cold, too thick and too rigid to tear apart.
items.title: An ancient failed rift is reawakening inside one of Africa's oldest landmasses

items.teaser: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.
items.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'

items.teaser: We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.
items.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
